passage: Twenty-year-old Valentina joined the vigil in the town square at dusk, holding a small candle in a paper cup. Hundreds of people had come to remember a teacher from the university who had died. Nobody gave a speech at first. Someone began to sing a quiet song, and voices joined in, some off-key. Diego, standing beside her, placed a white flower at the foot of the lamp post. Valentina did the same. She had no words for how heavy her chest felt, but lighting the candle, singing along and placing the flower gave the feeling a shape. When the crowd bowed their heads together, Valentina found that her own shoulders had dropped.

qa.q: What did Diego place at the foot of the lamp post?
qa.a: Diego placed a white flower at the foot of the lamp post.

qa.q: What was Valentina feeling in the square, and how do you know?
qa.a: Valentina felt a heavy sadness she had no words for, and the dropped shoulders at the end suggest the shared acts eased it.

qa.q: What choice did Valentina make in the square that helped, and why?
qa.a: Valentina lit the candle, sang along and placed a flower as the others did, and doing the same acts as everyone gave a shape to a feeling that had no words.

qa.q: What might the people who sang off-key have been feeling?
qa.a: They may have been more concerned with joining in than with sounding right, so singing together was more important than the tune.

grounding: A young adult takes part in a vigil and finds comfort in doing the same acts as others, since ritual gives shape to feelings without words.

passage: On the lawn of the college, the physics department held a memorial for Professor Mathur, who had taught there for thirty years. Students, staff and the canteen workers stood in a semicircle. A lamp was lit, and one by one people stepped forward to place a marigold at the photo. Jaya waited in line, hands cold. Zeenat, next to her, whispered a prayer in her own tradition. The silence lasted a full minute. Jaya, who had not cried when she heard the news, felt her eyes fill as she set down her flower. Later, in the queue for tea, nobody explained anything, but people stood close together, and Jaya found she could breathe again.

qa.q: How many years had Professor Mathur taught at the college?
qa.a: Professor Mathur had taught there for thirty years.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel as she placed the flower, and why only then?
qa.a: Jaya felt a wave of grief as her eyes filled, though she had not cried at the news; the shared act of placing the flower seems to have released it.

qa.q: What could Jaya do when the ceremony ends if sadness comes back later?
qa.a: Jaya could stay near people who were there, talk about the professor and take part in any further small remembrances.

qa.q: How might Zeenat's prayer in her own tradition sit beside Jaya's own way of mourning?
qa.a: Zeenat seems to grieve in a personal way while standing shoulder to shoulder with everyone, showing shared ritual can hold different traditions.

grounding: A young adult takes part in a memorial and finds comfort in doing the same acts as others.

passage: Zeynep hadn't known Professor Weber well, only from two lectures a week. But when the university announced his death, she went to the vigil on the library steps anyway. Three hundred students stood in the cold with paper cups around their candles. For the first minutes nobody made a speech. Then someone placed a pebble on the steps, and others followed, one by one. Zeynep didn't know the custom, but Kaito, from her seminar, handed her a small grey stone. She placed it beside his. When a choir student began to hum, the crowd joined in without words. Zeynep felt her chest loosen. She couldn't have explained what she felt, but her hands knew what to do.

qa.q: Where was the vigil held?
qa.a: On the library steps.

qa.q: What does 'her hands knew what to do' suggest about Zeynep's feelings?
qa.a: Zeynep felt a quiet comfort and belonging; the shared ritual gave shape to sadness she couldn't put into words.

qa.q: What helped Zeynep take part in a custom she didn't know?
qa.a: Kaito handing her a stone; offering a newcomer a simple way to join lets them share the ritual.

qa.q: How might Kaito experience handing Zeynep the stone?
qa.a: Kaito likely felt glad to include someone and less alone in grief, through a simple act that needed no words.

grounding: A young adult at a vigil finds comfort in doing the same small acts as others, giving shape to feelings without words.

passage: The girls' hostel common room had been turned into a prayer hall. Pooja's photo sat on a table, garlanded, with a diya beside it. She had died in a road accident on the way home for the holidays, and forty residents had come back early. Jasleen stood near the door, not sure what to do with her hands. The warden asked everyone to light a small candle from the diya, one after another. Trisha, beside her, whispered, 'I don't even know what I'm feeling.' 'Me neither,' Jasleen said. They lit their candles together. Someone started the hostel song they sang on Annual Day, and slowly everyone joined in, voices shaking. Jasleen found herself crying and singing at once, and it felt, strangely, like the right thing.

qa.q: How many residents had come back early?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: Why might crying and singing at once have felt right to Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen felt sad and comforted together; the shared song gave her grief a shape when she had no words.

qa.q: How did the warden help the residents mourn together?
qa.a: By giving everyone a simple shared act, lighting a candle from the diya one by one, so feelings without words had a form.

qa.q: What might Trisha have gained from lighting the candle with Jasleen?
qa.a: Trisha, unsure what she felt, likely felt less alone having someone to share the act with.

grounding: Young women at a hostel memorial find comfort in shared rituals of candle-lighting and song.

passage:
Dear Swati,
Thatha's funeral was last week. I thought I'd hate the rituals. I thought they'd feel like a show. But on the thirteenth day, when all of us, cousins and aunts and uncles, sat on the floor and passed the rice balls from hand to hand, something happened. Nobody spoke, but we were all doing the same thing at the same time, and I stopped feeling like I was drowning alone.
Amma cried while tying the flowers. I tied them with her. My cousin who never talks put his arm around me during the chanting.
I still don't have words for what I feel. The rituals gave my hands something to do while the words catch up.
Miss you. Call soon.
Keerthana

qa.q: What did the family pass from hand to hand on the thirteenth day?
qa.a: The rice balls.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel during the rice-ball ritual?
qa.a: Keerthana felt less alone and quietly comforted, no longer drowning alone while everyone did the same thing together.

qa.q: What might Keerthana do while the words 'catch up'?
qa.a: Keep joining simple rituals with family, like tying flowers with Amma, and talk to Swati when ready.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Keerthana tied the flowers with her?
qa.a: Amma was crying, so having Keerthana beside her likely felt comforting and made her grief feel shared.

grounding: A young adult finds that funeral rites shared with family give shape to grief that has no words yet.

passage: You asked why I went, even though I'm not a candle person. I'm Kiran, and honestly I didn't know what to do with any of it. Dr Nirmala Rao taught us statistics for two years, and then one Monday she was just gone. That evening about two hundred of us stood on the library steps. Someone handed me a candle. We didn't speak much. We sang the college song, slowly, and then the old film song she used to hum while marking. I don't sing. I sang. My hands stopped shaking once they had the candle to hold. When we set the candles down in rows, it looked like the lines on her graphs. I couldn't have made a speech that night. But I could light a wick like everyone else, and that was enough to carry it home.

qa.q: Where did the students gather that evening?
qa.a: They stood on the library steps.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel once the candle was in hand?
qa.a: Kiran felt steadier and comforted; the shaking stopped once there was something to hold and do alongside the others.

qa.q: Why might shared acts help when words fail, as they did for Kiran?
qa.a: Doing the same simple things as everyone, lighting, singing, placing candles, gave shape to grief that Kiran could not have put into a speech.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran had stayed away from the vigil?
qa.a: Kiran would likely have carried the loss alone, without the comfort of standing with two hundred others who felt it too.

grounding: Kiran finds comfort in a college vigil, where doing the same acts as others gives shape to grief without words.
